issues.legal_issue: A person accused of an offence under special legislation protecting Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes is not entitled to anticipatory bail when the complaint prima facie discloses that offence.
material_facts: The complainant alleged that the accused abused her and her family by referring to their caste and assaulted them after a dispute involving the flow of rainwater between agricultural fields.
The complaint specifically attributed to the group the statement that the complainant’s community should be beaten so that its members would not live in the village.
The complaint led to an accusation under the special legislation as well as offences under the Penal Code, and the accused sought anticipatory bail.
issues.conclusion: The specific allegations prima facie disclosed an offence under the special legislation, so the statutory bar applied and the accused were not entitled to anticipatory bail; the special leave petition was dismissed.
issues.legal_principle: Section 18 of the Scheduled Castes and the Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989 bars relief under Section 438 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 in a case involving an accusation of an offence under that Act, unless the court prima facie finds that such an offence is not made out. A specific complaint averment of insult or intimidation intended to humiliate by use of a caste name is relevant to that prima facie assessment. The Court said the cited High Court decisions—Dr. R.K. Sangwan v. State, M.A. Rashid v. Gopal Chandra, and Ramesh Prasad Bhanja v. State of Orissa—could not be treated as precedent against the statutory bar; the result depends on the complaint’s averments.

predicates.anticipatory_bail_proceeding: An accused sought release before arrest in a criminal proceeding.
predicates.protected_offence_accusation: The criminal accusation included an offence under legislation protecting Scheduled Castes or Scheduled Tribes.
predicates.prima_facie_protected_offence_disclosed: The complaint’s allegations, including a specific allegation of caste-based insult or intimidation intended to humiliate, disclosed an offence under that legislation on a prima facie assessment.

issues.definition: When an accused seeks release before arrest in a case alleging a protected-group offence, and the complaint prima facie discloses that offence, anticipatory bail is unavailable.

issues.legal_issue: A court deciding anticipatory bail in a case alleging an offence under special legislation protecting Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes must confine its assessment to whether the complaint prima facie discloses the offence and must not conduct a critical analysis of the evidence.
material_facts: The accused sought anticipatory bail in a case that included an accusation under the special legislation.
The Court considered the complaint’s specific allegations of caste-based abuse and assault in deciding whether the statutory bar applied.
issues.conclusion: The court’s inquiry is limited: it must verify whether the complaint prima facie makes out an offence and must not critically analyze the evidence or undertake an elaborate discussion of it.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 18 of the Scheduled Castes and the Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989 and 438 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 operate together to bar anticipatory bail where an offence under the special legislation is prima facie disclosed. In considering the application, the court’s scope to appreciate evidence and other material is limited; the Court relied on no earlier Supreme Court case for this proposition and stated that contrary High Court decisions cited by counsel could not be treated as precedent against the statutory bar.

predicates.anticipatory_bail_proceeding: An accused sought release before arrest in a criminal proceeding.
predicates.protected_offence_accusation: The criminal accusation included an offence under legislation protecting Scheduled Castes or Scheduled Tribes.

issues.definition: In an anticipatory-bail proceeding involving an accusation under protected-group legislation, the court confines its scrutiny to a prima facie assessment of whether the alleged offence is made out.
